passage: The hostel's wifi crawled, and Rashmi's phone showed one bar when Jeevan's message arrived: "WORST DAY EVER!!!!!!! 😭😭 I HATE EVERYTHING". She read it twice. Jeevan often wrote like that, once in capitals over a burnt toast, yet last week he had truly been stressed about his practical exam. With the signal cutting in and out, she couldn't hear his voice or see his face, so she couldn't tell which Jeevan had typed it. She walked to the corridor window, where the network was better, and called. "Hey, is this a play worst day or a real worst day?" He laughed. "Bit of both. I missed the bus, and the exam thing is still bugging me. Thanks for asking though."

qa.q: How many bars of signal did Rashmi's phone show?
qa.a: Her phone showed one bar.

qa.q: What was Rashmi worried about when she read Jeevan's message?
qa.a: She wasn't sure if the capitals and dramatic emojis were play or real distress, since Jeevan usually exaggerated but had been stressed about his practical exam.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that helped?
qa.a: She checked directly by calling and asking whether it was play or real, instead of guessing from the capitals.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see his own message?
qa.a: He may see it as half joke and half honest stress, and he may not realise how it looks from far away with no face or voice to read.

grounding: A teen writes in capitals with many exclamation marks and dramatic emojis, which may be play or real intensity, and a quick check helps.

passage: Himani posted a story that evening: "I CANNOT BELIEVE THIS!!!!!! 😱 my life is a disaster." Under it was a photo of her test paper. Within minutes people were reacting with laughing faces and "same!!". Pallavi, sitting in her own room, wasn't sure what to think. Himani had a habit of dramatic posts for her followers, and she also had a real habit of caring too much about marks. Pallavi typed a private message instead of joining the reactions: "Hey, is that a joke-dramatic or a really-upset one? I'm around either way." Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Then: "Honestly, a little of both. I'll call you in ten minutes." Pallavi put the phone down, relieved she'd asked.

qa.q: What did Himani's story show under the caption?
qa.a: It showed a photo of her test paper.

qa.q: What might Himani be feeling when she posts the story?
qa.a: Probably a mix of real upset about the marks and a wish to be seen and joined by her followers, and she admits it is a little of both.

qa.q: Why was a private message better than adding a reaction?
qa.a: The public reactions treated the post as a joke, while a private check gave Himani room to say if some of it was real.

qa.q: How might the followers have read the post differently from Pallavi?
qa.a: They only saw capitals and an emoji and took it as playful, while Pallavi knew Himani's habits and worried about the real feeling under it.

grounding: A teen's capitals and dramatic emoji may be play, real intensity or performing for followers, and a quick private check helps.

passage: Ganga arrived at school laughing at a video with her friends, so loud that the teacher, Farhan, looked over. By second period she was snapping at her desk partner for tapping a pen. After lunch she sat with her head down, and when Farhan asked whether she had finished the worksheet, her eyes filled and she whispered, "I can't do anything right." Fifteen minutes later she was giggling at a joke in the corridor. Farhan didn't remark on the swings or call her dramatic. He put a glass of water on her desk and said, "Take your time." Later he asked quietly whether she had been sleeping enough, and mentioned that the school counsellor was always around if she wanted a chat.

qa.q: What did Farhan put on Ganga's desk?
qa.a: He put a glass of water on her desk.

qa.q: What might Ganga be feeling as her mood moves from laughing to snapping to tearful?
qa.a: Her feelings may truly be shifting, from playful to irritated to discouraged within a few hours, and she may not understand why herself.

qa.q: How did Farhan support Ganga?
qa.a: He stayed calm and consistent, offered water, asked gently about sleep, and mentioned the counsellor, without calling her dramatic.

qa.q: How might Ganga's classmates experience her changing moods?
qa.a: They may find it confusing, like the desk partner who was snapped at, unless they remember that moods can swing a lot at her age.

grounding: A teen swings from laughing to irritable to tearful within hours, and patient consistency and gentle talk help.

passage:
Dear Anand bhaiya,
Sorry about how I've been at home. I know at breakfast I was laughing at everything, at lunch I snapped at you for taking the remote, and by night I was crying over a song I've heard fifty times. It's not you and I don't fully know why it happens. It just changes fast, like weather. Mummy says it's part of growing up, and I'm trying to sleep at a proper time because that seems to make it better. What helps most is when you don't make a big deal, and just say something normal or sit with me. Please keep doing that. I'll try to tell you when I need space.
Tarun

qa.q: What did Tarun snap at Anand for?
qa.a: He snapped at Anand for taking the remote.

qa.q: What does Tarun feel about his mood changes?
qa.a: He feels puzzled and sorry, since it isn't about Anand and he doesn't fully know why his mood changes as fast as weather.

qa.q: What does Tarun say helps him most?
qa.a: He says it helps when Anand doesn't make a big deal and just says something normal or sits with him.

qa.q: How might Anand feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and understood, since he learns the snapping wasn't personal and knows how to help.

grounding: A teen swings between laughing, irritable and tearful within a day, and calm consistency and gentle talk support balance.

passage:

passage: Manjula, you asked how I usually react when something goes wrong. Honestly, I shrug. "It's fine," I say, even when it's not. When my drawing wasn't picked for the school exhibition, I shrugged, went upstairs and drew for two hours. I don't like people fussing over me. It feels like too much attention and I never know what to say. My grandmother noticed anyway. She never asked me straight. She just said, "The kitchen light stays on late, and there's always something warm on the stove." That night I went down. I ate a bit, and then said, "I really wanted that one." She only nodded. I'm Devika, and I'm still a shrugger, but I know where the kitchen light is.

qa.q: What did Devika do for two hours after her drawing wasn't picked?
qa.a: She went upstairs and drew for two hours.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she said 'It's fine'?

qa.q: What did Devika's grandmother do that worked?
qa.a: She left the door open without pressing, saying the kitchen light stayed on late, so Devika could come when she was ready.

qa.q: How might Devika's grandmother have felt seeing her shrug?
qa.a: She probably worried a little but respected Devika's privacy, choosing to wait quietly instead of asking straight out.

grounding: A teen plays feelings down with a shrug and 'it's fine' to avoid drama, and a trusted adult leaves the door open.

passage:
"You laughed so loudly when you fell!" Darshan said, dropping onto the canteen bench beside Urmila. "You looked so confident."
"Confident?" She stared at him. "Darshan, I wanted the floor to swallow me. Forty people watched me trip on my own bag strap."
"But you got up, took a bow and everyone clapped."
"That's because I laughed first. If I hadn't, I think I'd have run out." She rubbed her elbow. "It was half funny, half horrible."
"I honestly thought you didn't care."
"I care about everything. That's the problem."
Darshan grinned and pushed his fries toward her. "Next time, I'll sit close. Deal?" She took one. "Deal."

qa.q: What did Urmila trip on?
qa.a: She tripped on her own bag strap.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling as she laughed loudly?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and afraid of looking foolish, and the laugh helped cover it and gave her relief, though part of it was truly funny.

qa.q: What could Darshan do next time a friend slips in public?
qa.a: He could stay close and check in afterwards, because a big laugh may be covering embarrassment rather than showing confidence.

qa.q: How did the onlookers likely read Urmila's laughter?
qa.a: They read it as confidence and clapped, so they missed how uncomfortable she felt.

grounding: A teen laughs loudly after a slip in front of others to cover embarrassment, and others read it as confidence.

passage: In Class 11 I once walked into the glass door of the physics lab in front of everyone. It made an actual thud. I remember the exact second: silence, then my own voice booming with laughter before anyone else's. I even said "Ta-da!" and waved. People cheered. Francis, who sat next to me, gave me a thumbs up and told me afterwards I was the most relaxed person he'd ever seen. I nodded as though I was. But my ears were burning, and I went to the toilets and stood there for five minutes, hands under cold water, feeling foolish and relieved at the same time. I still laugh first when I slip. I just know now what that laugh is. - Samir

qa.q: What did Samir walk into in front of everyone?
qa.a: He walked into the glass door of the physics lab.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he stood in the toilets?
qa.a: He felt foolish and relieved, since the loud laugh had covered his embarrassment and the room had accepted it.

qa.q: What could Samir tell Francis if he wanted to be understood?
qa.a: He could say that the laugh was covering embarrassment and that he wasn't as relaxed as he looked.

qa.q: How did Francis see Samir after the slip?
qa.a: He saw a very relaxed person, so he misread the laugh as confidence.

grounding: A teen laughs loudly after a slip to cover embarrassment, others read it as confidence, and the laugh may be relief.

passage: In the college corridor, a group was passing round the class results when someone said, loudly enough for everyone, "Naveen, did you get your marks from a lucky draw?" A couple of people laughed. Naveen laughed too, a wide, quick smile, and said, "Yeah, best draw of my life." He walked on without looking at anyone. Suraj noticed the smile didn't reach his eyes and that Naveen's fingers tightened round his folder. He didn't rush over or say "I know you're hurt." He just sent a message that evening: "That joke earlier was rubbish. You okay? No need to reply now." A reply came an hour later: "Thanks. It stung a bit." Suraj wrote back, "I'm here."

qa.q: What did someone ask Naveen about his marks?
qa.a: Someone asked, 'Did you get your marks from a lucky draw?'

qa.q: What might Naveen have been feeling behind his wide, quick smile?
qa.a: Probably hurt and a wish not to look weak, though Suraj can't be sure, and Naveen later admitted it stung a bit.

qa.q: Why did Suraj follow up privately instead of in front of everyone?
qa.a: A public comment could make Naveen feel more exposed, while a private message let him reply in his own time without pressure.

qa.q: How might the people who laughed have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have thought Naveen took the joke well, since he laughed too, and never realised it hurt.

grounding: A teen laughs off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak, and a friend gently follows up privately.

passage:
"Payal, you laughed when Kavya said that about your accent."
"Everyone did."
"I know, but you laughed the loudest." Indu sat on the hostel bed and folded her arms. "I'm not saying you're upset. I just wondered."
Payal turned her phone over in her hands. "It's just a joke."
"Okay. If it was, then that's fine. If it wasn't, I don't mind hearing it either."
There was a long pause. "It stung a bit," Payal said, quietly. "But I didn't want to be the girl who can't take a joke."
"You're allowed to be both."
Payal smiled properly this time. "Thanks for asking me alone. Not in front of them."

qa.q: Where were Indu and Payal talking?
qa.a: They were talking on the hostel bed.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she laughed at the accent joke?
qa.a: She felt hurt, since it stung a bit, but she laughed to avoid looking like someone who can't take a joke.

qa.q: What did Indu do well when she raised the topic?
qa.a: She asked privately, didn't assume, and said Payal could tell her either way, which made it safe to speak.

qa.q: How might Kavya have felt about the joke?
qa.a: Kavya may not have known it hurt, since Payal laughed along, and she might want to know so she can stop.

grounding: A teen smiles and laughs off a hurtful joke, and a friend follows up privately without assuming.

passage:
Day 1. Santosh arrived at the university in Helsinki and met his lab partner, Hansa, who listened to his introduction with an almost blank face and said, "Good." He felt his stomach sink, sure that she disliked him.
Day 4. Back home, everyone shows what they think on their face, so he read her calm expression as coldness. In the lab she hardly smiled, but she checked his calculations twice and stayed late to help.
Day 10. Santosh asked her directly, "Are you okay working with me? I can't tell." Hansa looked surprised. "Very much. I'm listening. A calm face is how I show respect here." They both laughed.

qa.q: Where did Santosh meet his lab partner?
qa.a: He met her at the university in Helsinki.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel when Hansa answered with an almost blank face?
qa.a: He felt anxious and rejected, and he took her calm face as a sign she disliked him.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that cleared things up?
qa.a: He asked Hansa directly whether she was okay working with him, instead of relying on stereotypes or guesses.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh read her calm face as coldness?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and a little sorry, since she was showing respect and care through help and listening, not through open expression.

grounding: A young adult abroad reads a restrained face as coldness, then learns by asking that it means respect and calm.

passage: "When I started at the plant in Osaka thirty years ago, Kalyani, I thought my supervisor hated me," Arnab said, pouring tea for his niece, who was packing for her exchange year. "Mr Tanaka never smiled when I proposed anything. He nodded once, wrote something down and said 'I will consider it.' I lay awake at night reading that as failure." He chuckled. "Months later I learned he put my ideas in the monthly meeting, and his still face was how he listened. A colleague explained it. I could have asked him myself, and saved myself many nights." Kalyani looked up. "So I should ask?" "Politely and directly, yes. And don't decide about a whole country from one face."

qa.q: Where did Arnab start working thirty years ago?
qa.a: He started at the plant in Osaka.

qa.q: What did Arnab feel about his supervisor's still face at first?
qa.a: He felt anxious and rejected, sure that he was failing and that his supervisor hated him.

qa.q: What advice does Arnab give Kalyani?
qa.a: To ask politely and directly when she can't read a face abroad, and not to judge a whole country from one expression.

qa.q: How might Mr Tanaka have seen his own behaviour?
qa.a: He may have thought he was being respectful and attentive by listening quietly and taking the ideas to the meeting.

grounding: A young adult working abroad finds a restrained face can mean respect, not coldness, and asking directly avoids stereotypes.

passage:
Day 1. Ayesha was on a video call with Keerthana, who was studying in another country. Halfway through her story, Keerthana's face froze on screen with a deep frown. Ayesha's heart sank. She thought she had said something wrong and quickly ended the call.
Day 3. Keerthana messaged: "Did I do something? You hung up." Ayesha explained about the frown. Keerthana laughed. "That was lag! The connection died and I was leaning in, trying to hear."
Day 8. They agreed that on calls they would say "You frozen?" or "I'm just concentrating!" instead of guessing from a paused picture. The next call, someone did freeze, and both laughed at it.

qa.q: What did Keerthana's face show when it froze on screen?
qa.a: It showed a deep frown.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel when the frozen frown appeared?
qa.a: She felt worried that she had said something wrong, and reacted by ending the call quickly.

qa.q: What did the friends agree to do to avoid misreading each other?

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when the call ended suddenly?
qa.a: She was probably confused and a little hurt, which is why she messaged to ask if she had done something.

grounding: A young adult reads a frozen video frame as a frown of displeasure when it was lag, and verbal check-ins are more reliable.

passage:
"Your uncle in Dubai rings you on video every Sunday, doesn't he?" Himani asked, and Sarita, her grandmother, smiled and settled into the cane chair.
"Yes, and one Sunday I nearly cried. He was talking, and the picture froze with his mouth half-open and his brows pulled together, as if he were angry or in trouble. The screen stayed like that for a full minute. I thought, something is wrong, he's hiding it from me." She laughed. "Then the sound came back and he said, 'Amma, the network is terrible!' He was squinting to hear me."
"What did you do?"
"Now I say 'How are you, really?' when I'm in doubt. A face on a screen is not the person."

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when the picture froze with his brows pulled together?

qa.q: What does Sarita now do when she isn't sure about someone on a call?
qa.a: She asks aloud how they really are, instead of inferring mood from a paused face.

qa.q: How might the uncle have felt on his side of the call?
qa.a: He was probably squinting to hear and frustrated by the network, unaware that his frozen face had frightened his mother.

grounding: A young adult reads a frozen video frame as bad news when it was a bad connection, and asking verbally is more reliable.

passage: Behind the counter of his family's small shop in the kasba, Uday had learned to watch smiles. The wholesaler, Harsha, came in each Tuesday and greeted him with a quick, tight smile that stopped at the mouth. The old woman who bought tea leaves gave a slow one that crinkled her eyes and stayed for a while. Uday used to think the first meant "I dislike you." Today he wasn't sure. Harsha looked tired, then dropped an extra packet of biscuits on the counter and said, "For the kids you tutor." That smile came late and quiet. Uday noted it: the face was only a clue. He still asked, "Long journey today?" "Very," Harsha said.

qa.a: Harsha comes in each Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Uday thinking about Harsha's tight smile?
qa.a: He used to read it as dislike, but now he sees it might just be tiredness, since Harsha then did something kind.

qa.q: Why did Uday ask 'Long journey today?'
qa.a: A smile alone is only a rough clue, so a friendly question helps him check what is actually going on.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the tight smile himself?
qa.a: He may simply be tired after travelling and not realise his smile looks polite and distant.

grounding: A young adult tells a polite mouth-only smile from a warm smile that involves the eyes, but treats it only as a rough clue.

passage: Bilal worked evenings at a small cafe in Warsaw, and he'd started noticing smiles the way some people notice weather. The manager's smile when she praised him was wide and instant, but it left her eyes untouched, and he wondered if it was only routine. A regular, Marek, gave a small smile, hardly more than a twitch, but it lasted and his eyes creased as he took his coffee. Bilal couldn't say which of the two was sincere. The manager's had felt fake, but she had actually given him a raise. Marek's quiet one had seemed genuine, and he had brought Bilal a jar of plum jam. He decided a smile was only a hint, and kept watching what people did.

qa.a: He worked evenings at a small cafe in Warsaw.

qa.q: What does Bilal suspect about the manager's smile, and why is he unsure?
qa.a: He wondered if her wide, instant smile was only routine, since her eyes were untouched, but he couldn't be sure because she had given him a raise.

qa.q: What did Bilal decide to do about reading smiles?
qa.a: He decided a smile is only a hint and kept watching what people actually did over time.

qa.q: How might Marek see his own small smile?
qa.a: He probably meant it warmly, though it was quiet, which shows that many genuine smiles are subtle.

grounding: A young adult compares a polite mouth-only smile with a warm eye-crinkling one, treating the difference as a rough clue only.

passage: When I moved to Berlin for my degree, I smiled at everyone on the train, the way I would in my town at home. Nobody smiled back. A man frowned; a woman looked at her shoes. I decided the city was cold and felt lonely. My classmate Dolma, who grew up in a hill town and had studied in Japan first, laughed when I told her. "Here, smiling at strangers is odd," she said. "In Japan, when I bumped into someone I smiled to say sorry, and I was embarrassed, and people knew that. It changes place to place." I started watching what locals did instead of guessing. Now I nod to neighbours, and they nod back. - Sahil

qa.q: Which city did Sahil move to for his degree?
qa.a: He moved to Berlin for his degree.

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when nobody smiled back on the train?
qa.a: He felt lonely and decided the city was cold, though the lack of smiles was really about local norms.

qa.q: What did Sahil change after talking to Dolma?
qa.a: He started watching what locals did instead of guessing, and began nodding to neighbours.

qa.q: How might the man who frowned have seen Sahil's smile?
qa.a: He may have found it unusual from a stranger, not unfriendly, since smiling at strangers is odd there.

grounding: A student in a new city finds smiling at strangers means different things in different places, so local norms matter.

passage: Advisor's note. Usha, an exchange student from Manila, met me today after her professor complained that she "smiled and seemed not to care" about a missed deadline. Here, the professor read her smile as being casual. I explained to Usha that many professors in this city expect an eye-contact apology in words.
